newsitem.title: USA: U.S. property insurers helped by mild winter in Q1.
newsitem.headline: U.S. property insurers helped by mild winter in Q1.

text.p: Most U.S. property-casualty insurers will post a roughly 20 percent increase in first quarter operating profits, helped by a mild winter, despite a major snowstorm on the last day of the quarter.

Although that storm may push first quarter catastrophe losses of $675 million somewhat higher, the quarter's losses will be nothing in comparison to last year's first quarter insured catastrophe losses of $2.5 billion.

"For the property-casualty companies, I think actually you could get some favorable comparisons because last year you had the blizzard and really horrible winter weather," Advest analyst Gloria Vogel said.
"I suspect that the comparisons will be good only because last year's first quarter was so bad," she said.
Operating earnings for property-casualty companies are expected to increase 21 percent, First Call director of research Chuck Hill said.
Multi-line insurers are expected to post a 20 percent increase in operating earnings and life insurers are expected to post a 17 percent increase, Hill said.
Commercial property-casualty insurers will begin to reap the benefits of one-time charges to strengthen reserves and restructuring actions taken last year, Lehman analyst Peter Wade said.
"Through 1996, many companies were restructuring their operations," Wade said, and analysts now have to estimate the positive impact of these actions.
"More often than not, investors err on the conservative side and underestimate the improvements that result from business restructurings," he said.

Insurers that strengthened reserves, removing the drag on ongoing earnings, or restructured operations last year include Allstate Corp, Chubb Corp, The Hartford, Travelers Property Casualty Corp and St. Paul Cos Inc, analysts said.
"I think we're going to have a very favorable earnings season for the large cap property-casualty companies, which is going to drive positive consensus revisions for this group," Wade said.
However, foreign exchange rates may restrain the profit growth of some large international insurers such as American International Group Inc because of the strength of the dollar, analysts said.
But the big problem is that the industry's fundamentals remain poor, with premium growth sluggish and pricing under pressure, J.P Morgan analyst James English said.
"Competitive conditions are really difficult, especially in commercial lines," English said.
"Premiums are just not growing rapidly at all," he said, as insurers try to avoid taking on new business at unattractive prices.
English said he would be satisfied with premium growth in the mid-single digit range.
Investors must "temper their judgment (about premium growth) by the notion that insurers could be putting on bad business if they are too aggressive in this market," he said.
And, he said, it will take a catastrophe worse than hurricanes Andrew and Iniki in 1992 to turn the commercial property-casualty market around.
A catastrophic event would "have to be significant to create enough withdrawal of capacity to change the pricing on the commercial side," he said.
